# Diagnosing CV Joint Noise on a 1990 Honda Accord EX

A rhythmic clunking sound during tight turns is indeed the classic symptom of a worn outer Constant Velocity (CV) joint. On your 1990 Honda Accord EX, this noise occurs because the joint has lost its ability to maintain constant rotational speed across varying angles. When you turn sharply, the drivetrain flexes, and if the internal ball bearings or races are compromised, they skip against each other under load, creating that distinct "click-clack" rhythm. The fact that the noise is specific to turns rather than acceleration confirms the issue lies with an outer joint; inner joints typically whine during hard acceleration from a stop.

Your visual inspection of the axle boots was the right first step. A torn boot allows grease to escape and contaminants like road salt and grit to enter, which accelerates wear. While you noted no holes on either side, the observation that one assembly appears visibly older is a strong heuristic indicator. In vehicles of this era, rubber deterioration is often uneven due to exposure history or manufacturing variances. If one boot has been leaking for years while the other remained intact until recently, the older axle will almost certainly have degraded grease and worn internals. However, visual age alone isn't definitive proof of failure; a boot can remain sealed while the joint inside it degrades from initial poor lubrication or impact damage.

To move beyond speculation, you need to perform a physical load test on the axles with the wheels still off the ground. This is where most DIY diagnostics fail: relying solely on listening for noise while spinning the tires in place. That method only tests bearing smoothness and doesn't replicate the stress of a turn. Instead, stand behind the vehicle or have someone assist you to safely lift the car so all four wheels are supported by jack stands.

With the vehicle raised, grab the axle shaft itself—do not hold the wheel—and rotate it manually while applying lateral pressure. Simultaneously, ask your assistant to gently rock the suspension or have them turn the steering wheel slightly left and right while you apply force to the shaft near the differential end. You are looking for play in the joint's angles or a gritty feeling that resists smooth rotation. If one side feels rougher or has more axial play than the other, that is your culprit. Alternatively, spin each axle individually by hand with the wheels off and listen closely. A worn joint often emits a clicking sound even without steering input if the internal clearance is excessive enough to cause bearing skip at high RPMs, though this is less common than noise under load.

Once you have isolated the side, replacement requires removing the wheel, tie rod end, strut assembly (or lower control arm depending on your specific Accord sub-model), and then pulling the axle out from inside the engine bay. On many 1990 Accords, the inner joint is press-fitted into the differential housing, so you cannot reuse an old outer shaft if you need to swap just one side; you must replace the entire axle assembly or carefully transfer the hub and wheel bearing from the good side to the bad side, though transferring bearings is risky due to potential damage during removal.

Replacing both axles simultaneously is often the pragmatic choice for a 34-year-old vehicle. It prevents future labor costs if one wears out again next season and ensures balanced handling characteristics. While aftermarket options exist, sticking with OEM-spec parts or reputable brands like TRQ or Centric usually yields better longevity on older Honda chassis than budget aftermarket alternatives found at big-box retailers. If you choose to handle this yourself, ensure you have a torque wrench and the correct socket sizes for the axle nuts, which can be stubborn due to rust; penetrating oil applied well before attempting removal is essential.
